name: Natural Antisense Transcript (NAT) Knockdown (AntagoNAT)
therapeuticGoalDescription: Increase expression of an endogenous protein-coding gene by inhibiting its regulatory natural antisense transcript (NAT).
molecularDefect: Diseases caused by reduced gene expression or haploinsufficiency where a NAT negatively regulates the corresponding sense transcript.
diseaseMechanism: A natural antisense transcript represses expression of the sense gene through transcriptional, post-transcriptional, or epigenetic regulatory mechanisms. Blocking the NAT relieves repression and increases expression of the target gene.
suitableVariantTypes: Haploinsufficiency; reduced gene expression; loss-of-function disorders where a disease-relevant NAT has been experimentally demonstrated.
typicalDiseases: Angelman syndrome (UBE3A); Dravet syndrome (SCN1A, investigational); Friedreich's ataxia (investigational); additional neurological disorders under preclinical investigation.
rnaTargetRegion: Natural antisense transcript (lncRNA), typically overlapping promoter, exon, intron, or untranslated regions of the sense gene depending on NAT architecture.
transcriptRequirement: A validated disease-associated NAT regulating the target gene must be identified.
asoChemistry: RNase H-active gapmers (commonly phosphorothioate gapmers with 2′-MOE/LNA modifications) designed to degrade the NAT transcript.
typicalLength: Typically 16–20 nucleotides for RNase H-active gapmers; varies by chemistry and target.
designRules: Literature synthesis: identify the functional NAT; target accessible regions of the NAT; preserve specificity for the antisense transcript; experimentally validate gene upregulation.
secondaryStructureRequirement: Prefer accessible regions within the NAT transcript to facilitate efficient ASO binding.
offTargetConsiderations: Potential hybridization with unintended lncRNAs or overlapping transcripts; evaluate transcriptome-wide complementarity and unintended effects on neighboring genes.
advantages: Upregulates the endogenous gene without introducing exogenous DNA; preserves native regulation; particularly attractive for haploinsufficiency disorders.
limitations: Applicable only when a functionally relevant NAT has been identified; NAT biology remains incompletely characterized for many genes; mechanism may differ between loci.
clinicalTrialExamples: Angelman syndrome ASO programs targeting UBE3A-ATS; additional investigational NAT-targeting programs in neurological disorders.

evidenceLevel.note: Strong biological rationale and preclinical evidence; limited clinical validation.

referencesSummary: Modarresi et al. (2012); Wahlestedt (2013); Khorkova et al. (2022); Ali et al. (2024).
